doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Swing eighths versus straight Cuban articulation
summary: He explains articulation differences between swing and Cuban rhythms such as cha-cha-cha, and why the feel must be learned.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah. It seems like balancing those things you described has to take into account swinging eighth notes [scats] with balancing that with the Afro-Cuban rhythms that you mentioned. Is that a fair statement?
Say that again? It’s a what?
When I think of straight ahead I think of swing.
Yeah. The swinging the notes, the uneven [scats] uneven eighth notes, so balancing that with Afro-Cuban rhythms is, I guess, what you bring to the table.
Yeah. And that’s something that I explain when I go to colleges and universities, the difference of the articulation. Because when you play swing you swing the notes [scats]. Right?

Now we play the same tune Latin, like everybody calls it Latin and I don’t like that Latin, it’s Cuban rhythms, now you call that straight [counts/scats]. The articulation should be different. Should be different. And that’s what differentiates. But also what I have been doing, it’s something that occurs to me I think I like to mix — okay, you swing and I’m going to play straight eighths and let’s see what happens. Let’s see where we can go, how far can we go? But yeah, it is very simple. You swing [scats] and when you play a Cuban rhythm called cha-cha-cha you go [scats] one-two-three-four [scats]. When people, I always tell my, I used to tell my American colleagues the minute that you stop playing

Latin music and you start swinging your ride cymbal or you play swinging beats with your bass drums the flavor goes away, the flavor goes away. It’s like the way you play when you see someone who’s trying to swing and he doesn’t swing. You see somebody trying to do [scats] and what you hear is [scats] stiffed. It doesn’t swing. So the same way, the same thing happens the other way around. And that’s something that we have to, it’s something like yeah, I think in my opinion that is a gift that you bring, like when we musicians said either you have it or you don’t. That’s it. “He doesn’t have it.” Okay. But even if you have it, if you have that, you have to learn. It’s not okay, you’re going to see Monk playing this rhythm and you’re going to videotape and you’re going to go home, oh I can play — no — you’re playing a pattern but you’re not playing the music, you’re not playing the way it should be played. You don’t know about, you have to learn, you have to absorb that. You know what I mean?
